interstellar-ships.essay:
The nearest star system beyond the Sun, Alpha Centauri, is 4.34 to 4.37 light-years away. A light-year is the distance light covers in a year, so a radio message would take more than four years to get there and the same to come back. A ship that could carry people there would have to travel for a very long time. Designers therefore describe a generation ship, also called a worldship, in which people would live and die during the trip and their descendants would arrive. One report on a recent design competition describes a voyage of 250 years. No such ship exists. Crewed ships exist only as studies and paper designs.

Anyone hoping such a ship could leave every country behind first needs to understand how the law treats a ship once it has left. A ship built to travel to another star would stay under the legal control of the country that lists it on its official register of space objects. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, took effect on 10 October 1967, and 118 countries had joined it as of October 2025. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it "while in outer space" or on a natural body in space. It gives no distance at which this ends.

Read literally, that means the ship carries its registering country's law with it for as long as the voyage lasts. A person born aboard, a century out, would appear to come under the authority of a government that person had never seen. The treaty speaks of "personnel", which is an odd word for a child born on a ship, and it does not mention birth, so whether the word covers such a child is uncertain. The meaning of the word is unclear even for ordinary visitors. One commentary on whose law applies in a lunar habitat suggests that personnel may mean the operator's employees, so that paying visitors may fall outside the article and would have to be bound to the rules by contract. On that narrow reading, a child born aboard would be even less clearly covered. No court or government agency is known to have applied these articles to a voyage between stars, and no one has ruled on what happens to law on a voyage lasting many generations.

Two other articles apply before and during the trip. Article VI says private space activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that the country answers internationally for that activity. Article VII says countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage their space objects cause. These rules explain why the obstacle comes before departure. A private launch needs a country's approval. In the United States, that means a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million and the power to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. A group wanting to leave all governments must therefore first persuade one government to approve, register and take responsibility for it. No known project has reached that stage.

The real projects are studies. Project Hyperion was started by the researcher Andreas Hein in December 2011 from a student group at the Technical University of Munich. Its team published a study in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. A design competition opened in 2024, with results in July 2025, and first place went to the Italian team Chrysalis. Reports do not say how such a ship would be governed.

Icarus Interstellar, a volunteer nonprofit registered in Alaska in February 2011, aims at interstellar flight before the year 2100. Its project Persephone is a design concept for a worldship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. Its activity after 2015 is not known, and it has built no ship.

The 100 Year Starship began in 2010 at DARPA, the US military's research agency, which gave it $1 million, with $100,000 from NASA's Ames center. A workshop in January 2011 listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate problems. In 2012 a group led by the foundation of the former astronaut Mae Jemison won a $500,000 grant and took over the name, moving the project from government to private hands. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful federal spending projects. The last activity reported was a symposium in Nairobi in 2023.

Breakthrough Starshot, the one funded plan, carries no people. The investor Yuri Milner announced it in 2016. About 1,000 probes of a few grams each would ride on sails pushed by lasers on the ground, reaching 15 to 20 percent of the speed of light and arriving in 20 to 30 years. It began with US$100 million, with the final cost put at $5 billion to $10 billion. In September 2025 Scientific American reported it was on hold indefinitely, and the physicist Philip Lubin estimated that about $4.5 million had been spent. No formal cancellation has been reported. That final cost estimate is for probes of a few grams each.

Suppose a crewed ship were somehow funded and approved. The questions then follow in order. Before departure come the licence, the register, the radio frequencies coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries, and the question of who insures a craft that never returns. During the trip, no rescue is possible. Article V of the treaty asks astronauts to help each other, and no one else would be near. Everything must be made and recycled aboard. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, still relies on deliveries. The population must be large enough to stay healthy. The researchers F. Marin and C. Beluffi calculated in 2018 that 98 people gave a 100 percent success rate in their simulations of a 6,300-year trip to the planet Proxima Centauri b. Those aboard would need doctors, engineers and teachers from among themselves in every generation.

Governance is where the legal theory and practical reality separate. The ship's officers would be under the registering country's law, and a crime aboard would in theory fall under that country's courts. In practice, no police could reach them, and a message asking for instructions would take years once the ship neared another star. This is why the chance of holding on once under way is estimated as high, about 50 percent. It reflects distance alone. Children aboard would be subject to a law they never chose, though no outside authority could enforce it. The treaty's Article XVI lets a country withdraw on one year's notice, and countries can change or cease over a period of centuries. What would happen to a ship's legal status in such a case has not been addressed.

A common misunderstanding is that leaving the solar system means leaving the law. On paper it does not. Another is that a ship's company could become a nation on departure. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, asks for a defined territory, and a ship in motion has none. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent, as is the chance of building a crewed ship at all.

The most workable version today is the one already happening, namely research papers, design contests and small probes on paper, carried out under ordinary law on Earth. A crewed voyage would need a sponsoring country, which would keep legal control for as long as it and the treaty last.

outer-moons.essay:
Beyond Mars and the asteroid belt lie the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn, each with many moons, and smaller worlds called dwarf planets, such as Ceres in the asteroid belt. Some of these bodies are large and hold huge amounts of ice. Writers and engineers have suggested them as settlement sites because they could supply water, fuel and building materials on the spot. All such plans are studies on paper. No crew has been sent under any of them, and nobody has carried people this far.

Each world poses different physical problems, so a few figures help. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has ice over a hidden ocean that may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans. Its radiation is the main barrier, about 5.40 sieverts per day for an unshielded person, when about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal. A sievert is a measure of radiation dose. Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, receives about 0.08 sieverts per day and has gravity about 0.15 of Earth's. Callisto lies outside Jupiter's radiation belt, the zone of harmful radiation around the planet, and has gravity about 0.13 of Earth's. Titan, a moon of Saturn, has gravity 0.138 of Earth's, a thick atmosphere of nitrogen and methane, and lakes of hydrocarbons, but extreme cold and no free oxygen. Enceladus, also a moon of Saturn, has an underground ocean. A 2016 analysis of data from the Cassini spacecraft put the ice above it at 18 to 22 kilometres thick on average and less than 5 kilometres in the south polar region. Gravity this low has unknown effects on bone, muscle and children's growth.

The legal position is short and the same everywhere here. Nobody owns these worlds. They are natural bodies in space, so they fall under the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article II says they cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority, by using or occupying them, or by any other means. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country. Article VIII says the country that registers a craft keeps legal power over it and its crew, in space or on any natural body. The treaty text sets no distance limit on either rule. Since no craft has carried people this far, none of this has been tested. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with 17 members, also extends its ban on owning the surface to other bodies in the solar system, though only for those members.

Contamination is a further issue here. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds. COSPAR, an international committee of space scientists, issues a policy on protecting other worlds, and its January 2026 version added a unified policy for icy worlds. Oceans under ice are places where scientists hope to look for life, so a mission to drill into Europa or Enceladus would expect close questions from its licensing country and from its national space agency. COSPAR's policy has no treaty force of its own and works through those agencies.

The published descriptions of these settlement plans do not discuss ownership or law at all. They are engineering studies. Robert Zubrin, an American aerospace engineer who founded the Mars Society, wrote in his 1999 book Entering Space that Titan was the best moon for a base. Stephen Gillett had written about Titan as a home for life in the magazine Analog in 1992. Titan's atmosphere could supply a gas for making breathing air, and water beneath the surface could yield oxygen. In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, with igloos on the surface as bases for drilling, and possibly people living in air pockets inside the ice. Metals and minerals would have to be brought in, heavy shielding would be needed, and the plan was never carried out. In 2003 NASA's HOPE study, short for Revolutionary Concepts for Human Outer Planet Exploration, chose Callisto. A base there could make fuel for further exploration, and it has accessible water, silicate rock and metals. A crew's round trip was estimated at about 2 to 5 years, assuming major advances in propulsion. It stopped at the study stage.

The fourth case points to a different kind of settlement. In 2020 the Finnish space physicist Pekka Janhunen posted a preprint, a paper shared before formal publication, on a settlement in high orbit around Ceres. He chose Ceres for its nitrogen, which an Earth-like atmosphere requires. Spinning habitats joined to a disk-shaped frame would give the same gravity as Earth, mirrors would bring in sunlight, and a space elevator on Ceres would lift material cheaply. Density would stay at 500 people per square kilometre, on soil 1.5 metres deep. Each person would account for about 10 million kilograms of material. An orbiting structure of this kind would presumably be treated as a space object, though it would be built from Ceres materials and never launched from Earth. Who would register it is uncertain, because the Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects, speaks of objects launched into space. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty does mention objects "landed or constructed on a celestial body", but only in the sentence saying that ownership of such objects is unaffected by where they are. Its sentence on legal power speaks of an object "launched into outer space". Reading the text, it seems the drafters had things built on a natural body in mind for ownership and left open who holds legal power over something built from local material.

Suppose a private group tried. The first step would happen on Earth, as for any space mission. It would need a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million, and the launching country stays liable for damage. Frequencies would need filing through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. These steps all happen before the group leaves, so the group cannot avoid them by distance.

The next bumps are the voyage and supplies. Radio messages would take many minutes each way, so no one could call for instructions in an emergency. Travel would take years, which would keep other states away and also make rescue impossible. The treaty's Article V asks astronauts of member countries to help each other, which is of little use when no one is close. A doctor, a surgeon, teachers and engineers would all need to be aboard. Nothing delivered from Earth would arrive soon, and a resident could not easily leave. Children born there would have no choice in the matter, and they would be growing up in a gravity whose effects are unknown. Their nationality would depend on their parents' home countries, since the treaty does not mention birth. Americans would still have US tax duties on paper, whatever their distance.

Common misunderstandings concern distance again. Being very far away does not end the registering country's legal power, because the treaty sets no limit. Being first on Titan does not create a claim to it, because Article II bars that and Article I keeps all areas open to everyone. A self-declared nation would still lack a defined territory, one of the four tests of statehood in the Montevideo Convention of 1933. Recognition is estimated at about 0.1 percent.

The most workable version is a research base licensed by a treaty country, on a low-radiation world such as Callisto, as NASA's study suggested, and supplied by machines sent ahead. That study assumed major advances in propulsion. The chance of building is estimated at about 0.5 percent. Once a crew had arrived, distance would give them a fairly high practical chance of being left alone, estimated at about 40 percent. The same distance would make rescue impossible, and the law would continue to treat them as under the country that registered them.

venus-clouds.essay:
Venus is the planet next to Earth on the side nearer the Sun. Its surface is about 464 C, hotter than the melting point of lead, under an atmosphere pressing about 91 times as hard as Earth's air at sea level. Higher up, conditions change. About 50 to 55 kilometres above the ground, the temperature and air pressure come close to those on Earth. This has led engineers to propose living there in craft that float, without ever touching the ground. So a territory on Venus would mean a group of balloons or airships drifting in the clouds of another planet.

The physics explains the appeal. The atmosphere of Venus is mostly carbon dioxide, which is heavier than the mix of oxygen and nitrogen people breathe. Breathable air therefore floats there, in the same way that helium floats on Earth, with over 60 percent of the lifting power helium has on Earth. A balloon could hold the residents' own breathing air and be lifted by it. According to NASA's HAVOC study, at 55 kilometres the temperature is 27 C, the air pressure 0.5 bar (about half that at sea level on Earth) and gravity 8.73 metres per second squared, a little below Earth's. Figures from the NASA scientist Geoffrey Landis put about 50 kilometres at a pressure about the same as sea level on Earth, with temperatures of 0 to 50 C. A person going outside would need breathing air and protection from acid and some heat, and no pressure suit. A tear in the balloon would let gases mix slowly, leaving time for repairs, because the pressure is about equal on both sides. Landis argued that the atmosphere above would also shield against radiation about as well as Earth's does.

The difficulties are equally physical. The clouds contain sulfuric acid, so every outer surface must resist it. Winds at the cloud tops reach up to 95 metres per second, about 340 kilometres per hour, circling the planet about every four Earth days, and a floating city would travel with them, since tethering it would put stress on the structure. Hydrogen is very rare on Venus, which limits local water. Metals and other solid materials would have to be brought in or obtained some other way. The only human-made craft known to have floated there are the Soviet Union's Vega balloons, from 1985, and those small balloons lasted only days, until their batteries ran out.

The law is that of outer space generally. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article II that outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Nobody therefore owns Venus or its air. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and countries answer for what their nationals do. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body. Since nothing has been built there, no one has tested whether a balloon drifting in the air of Venus counts as a space object or as use of the planet. The treaty text speaks of objects launched into space and of natural bodies. A balloon launched from Earth and carrying its passengers fits those words reasonably well. A city built there from materials gathered on site raises a harder question that has no answer yet. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty does mention objects "landed or constructed on a celestial body", but only in the sentence saying that ownership of such objects is unaffected by where they are. Its sentence on legal power speaks of an object "launched into outer space". Reading the text, it seems the drafters had things built on a natural body in mind for ownership and left open who holds legal power over something built from local material.

Three proposals make up the record. In 1971 the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky proposed the Floating Islands of Venus, cities kept up some 50 or 60 kilometres high using technology from zeppelins and hot air balloons. He is not known to have claimed any part of Venus. In 2003 Landis presented his paper Colonization of Venus at a conference in Albuquerque. He argued that the only trouble with Venus is that the ground lies too far below the comfortable level, so settlers should live in the air. At the far extreme, aerostats, meaning craft that float like balloons, might cover the whole planet. In 2014 Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers at NASA's Langley Research Center, created HAVOC, the High Altitude Venus Operational Concept. It ran in five phases, from a robot airship 31 metres long to astronauts in orbit, a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 metres long, a one-year stay, and a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total. NASA later said it was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a real mission. It received no further funding and was cancelled by 2017. None of these proposals dealt with who would govern the residents.

Suppose a private group wants to build one floating station. Before anything else it needs a launching country, a licence and an entry on a register. In the United States, the licence comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance for harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the station and its staff, however far away they are. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. Contamination comes next. Article IX requires countries to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds, and the licensing country may apply that to a private crew.

Money is the next bump. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, so a year's food for one person, about 1,000 kilograms, would cost about $3.3 million to lift that far, and Venus is much farther. No private funding for this is known. Each resident needs about 0.84 kilograms of oxygen a day and much more in food and water. A breakdown would be serious, because a return trip takes months and there is no ground to land on. Medical care would be whatever is aboard. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, depends on other crews and countries being able to reach the spot, and none could for months. A crime aboard would fall under the registering country's law, and citizens would stay subject to their home country's rules, including US tax returns for Americans.

A common misunderstanding is that floating avoids the ban on occupying a planet. Article II says "by any other means", so a country or its licensed company gains no claim by floating. Another is that a floating city could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A craft blown around the planet by winds of 340 kilometres per hour has no fixed area, and no one may claim the air it moves through.

The most workable version is a small research airship under one country's licence, with robots first, along the path HAVOC described. Distance would slow any outside control, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 35 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent. In law it would stay a registered craft, the property of its owner, under the registering country.

asteroids.essay:
An asteroid is a lump of rock, metal or ice that orbits the Sun on its own. Asteroids range from boulders to small worlds, and most have very weak gravity. People are interested in them for two reasons. They might be mined for materials such as water ice, and in theory someone might one day hollow one out or build on one. No one has lived on an asteroid, and no funded plan to settle one is known. The nearest published proposal is a 2020 paper by the Finnish physicist Pekka Janhunen on a settlement in orbit around Ceres, the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt, and it remains on paper.

The law treats an asteroid the same way it treats the Moon. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, covers all natural bodies in space. Article II says no country may take one over by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means. Under Article VI, a private group needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty country, and that country answers for it. Under Article VIII, a craft stays under the law of the country that registered it, even after it lands. The Moon Agreement, a separate treaty that few countries have joined, applies its Moon rules to other bodies in the solar system except Earth. Those rules include a ban on private ownership of the surface. Its Article 1(3) says they do not apply to meteorites that reach Earth naturally, so a rock that falls in your field is a separate matter.

The best-known claim shows how this works in practice. Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Nevada, claimed the asteroid Eros in March 2000 because he wanted to establish that private people can own property in space. On 12 February 2001, NASA landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. NASA refused, saying his claim had no basis in law. He wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view Article II rules out private ownership of an asteroid. In November 2003 he asked a federal court in Reno to decide the matter. The judge ordered the case dismissed in April 2004, and the claim was dismissed on appeal in 2005. No court gave him title, and the lasting product of the case is an official American position against private ownership of an asteroid.

Paper claims continue anyway. A statement by the International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, says deed claims have been extended to other natural bodies in space, and one deed seller told Discover magazine that he owns about 95 planetary bodies. Fraud has appeared here too. In 1999, officials at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, listed share offerings for exploring a near-Earth asteroid among fraudulent internet schemes.

The real legal development concerns what is dug out of an asteroid, as opposed to the asteroid itself. A useful comparison is fishing on the open sea. No one owns the ocean, yet a boat owns the fish it catches. The United States adopted this reasoning in 2015. Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, now 51 USC 51303, says an American citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource may own, transport, use and sell it, subject to American law and the international obligations of the US. The law also disclaims any national ownership of a body in space. Luxembourg passed a similar law on 20 July 2017, and its own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. The United Arab Emirates followed with Federal Law No. 12 of 2019, and Japan with Act No. 83 of 2021. Section 10 of the Artemis Accords, a set of principles that countries sign as a political commitment, says extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated, and no court has tested any of these laws. The debate has moved to the UN's space committee, COPUOS, whose working group on space resources published a consolidated draft of principles in September 2026, with non-binding status and negotiations still running towards an April 2027 session. Its Principle 2 says extraction that complies with the Outer Space Treaty "does not inherently constitute national appropriation". The draft does not say who holds title to extracted material or what effect national laws have abroad. Russia pressed for treating resources "in place" as part of outer space and had earlier suggested a moratorium on their use, which is not in that draft. The United States, Canada and the United Kingdom objected to the word "shall" in non-binding principles. None of them gives anyone ownership of the asteroid.

Suppose a company in one of those countries sets out to mine an asteroid and house workers there. It first needs a launch licence. In the United States that comes from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The craft must go on a country's register under the Registration Convention, a treaty on listing objects launched into space, and private people have no way to register themselves. That country then keeps legal power over the craft and the people aboard. Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. If the craft damages something, the Liability Convention makes the launching country pay, so that country has good reason to demand insurance and supervision.

The next problem is money. Planetary Resources announced itself in 2012, and Deep Space Industries nine months later. Both built small spacecraft and both stood to gain from the new laws. Neither mined anything. A later start-up, AstroForge, launched the small test satellite Brokkr-1 in April 2023, and that mission failed because of communication problems. Its probe Odin, launched on 27 February 2025 to fly past the asteroid 2022 OB5, was declared lost on 6 March 2025. A further craft, DeepSpace-2, was planned for launch in the second half of 2026. A funding round for Planetary Resources with a major mining company fell through in 2017, which led to large layoffs, and in October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms. Bradford Space announced on 1 January 2019 that it had bought Deep Space Industries, by then working on small-satellite engines. The writer Jeff Foust concluded that the boom had been a bubble. Japan's Hayabusa 2 brought back a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020. Transport costs make the difficulty clear. A Falcon 9 rocket delivers cargo to low Earth orbit at about $3,246 per kilogram, and that is only the first and cheapest part of a trip to an asteroid. Supplying one person with food alone, about 1,000 kilograms a year, would cost about $3.3 million at that low-orbit rate, by simple arithmetic.

People who did reach an asteroid would meet further bumps. A claimed asteroid gives no right to exclude others. Article I of the treaty keeps all of space open to every country, and Article XII opens stations on natural bodies to visits by other members' representatives, on a basis of reciprocity and with advance notice. Help in an emergency could be months or years away, depending on the asteroid's path. Crime would remain under the law of the registering country and of people's home countries. Americans would still owe US tax returns, because the duty follows citizenship. A person who signs up to a self-declared asteroid nation changes none of this.

Common misunderstandings come from mixing up these layers. Owning ore is often reported as owning the asteroid. A national mining law is often taken to mean that the country has claimed territory, when these laws go out of their way to deny that. A deed from a website is taken for a title, and an invoice like Nemitz's is taken for a legal claim. The Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for statehood, asks for a defined territory, and Article II denies that to anyone on an asteroid.

The most workable version is a licensed robotic mining company based in a country with one of these laws, which owns what it extracts and sells it under that country's law. A crewed base would follow the same pattern, with staff living aboard a registered craft under the registering country's authority. Distance would make outside control slow, which is why holding on once there is estimated at about 30 percent, while the chance of building at all is estimated at about 1 percent. Under such a law a company could own its machines and its ore, and nobody would own the asteroid.

lagrange-cislunar.essay:
The space between Earth and the Moon is sometimes called cislunar space, meaning "on this side of the Moon". It has no ground. Anything placed there is a craft that keeps moving, and the Moon itself, about 385,000 kilometres from Earth, is the far edge of the region. Within it, and in the wider neighbourhood of Earth's path around the Sun, are special positions called Lagrange points. They are named after a mathematician, and they are places where the pull of two large bodies, such as the Earth and the Sun or the Earth and the Moon, balances in a way that lets an object keep its position relative to them while using little fuel.

NASA describes five such points for any pair of large bodies. Three of the five, called L1, L2 and L3, are like a ball balanced on the top of a steep hill. Any small push moves an object away, so a craft there needs constant small adjustments to stay in place. The other two, L4 and L5, are like a ball in a bowl. If an object there is pushed a little, it tends to return. L4 and L5 sit 60 degrees ahead of and behind the smaller body along its orbit. A point is a mathematical position, and nothing about it can be fenced or occupied the way a piece of land can. For the Earth and the Sun, NASA puts the first and second points about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, which is roughly four times the distance to the Moon.

The law here is the ordinary law of outer space, and no separate treaty covers this region. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, makes space free for all to use in Article I and bars any country from taking it over in Article II. Article VI makes countries responsible for space activity, including private activity, which needs their permission and continuing oversight. Article VIII gives legal power over a craft, and over the people aboard, to the country that registered it. Being at a Lagrange point changes none of that, so a craft at L5 is in the same legal position as a craft in low orbit. Two operators who both want to be near L5 have only the general duty of Article IX, which asks each country to pay due attention to the interests of others.

Two further documents add detail for some countries. The Moon Agreement, a treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system, says in Article 1(2) that references to the Moon include orbits and paths around it. Its rules, including its treatment of the Moon as the common heritage of mankind, therefore reach parts of this space, but only for the 17 countries that have joined it. The Artemis Accords, a set of principles for space activity, ask signing countries to register their objects (Section 7), release scientific data (Section 8), and give notice of operations inside "safety zones" to avoid harmful interference (Section 11). Section 1 names "the Lagrangian points for the Earth-Moon system" among the places they cover, and it limits them to civil activities of the signers' space agencies. The Accords describe themselves as a political commitment, so they do not create rights that a court could enforce.

The idea of living at these points has a real history. In September 1974 the physicist Gerard O'Neill published "The Colonization of Space" in the magazine Physics Today, describing colonies at Lagrange points. Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson, Arizona, read it and wrote to him, and in August 1975 they incorporated the L5 Society, named after the point. Its first newsletter set the long-range goal of disbanding at a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier followed in 1977. No hardware was ever built, and critics said transport costs were far too high for individuals to pay. The society's real effect was political. In 1979 and 1980 it campaigned against the Moon Agreement, arguing that treating the Moon's resources as the shared property of humanity would make space colonies impossible, and the United States never ratified that treaty. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates. Later work on a design called Kalpana One reflects a change of view. The Moon's L4 and L5 points are now thought too far from the Moon and Earth, and a settlement there would spend about two-thirds of its time outside the protection of Earth's magnetic field.

Suppose a private group wants to put a small habitat at the Earth-Moon L5 point. The group needs a launching country and an entry on that country's register, in the same way as a station in low orbit. In the United States, a launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration, with insurance against harm to others of up to $500 million. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, gives private people no way to register themselves. Whichever country registers the habitat then holds legal power over it and everyone inside.

The second step is radio. The habitat must talk to Earth, and the frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency whose members are countries. A national authority must file on the group's behalf, and that gives that country's regulator a say over the project. Supplies are the third step. The habitat depends on Earth for radio frequencies and for deliveries, and supply runs here would be harder than to low orbit. A Falcon 9 rocket costs about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit alone, and a person needs about 2.77 kilograms of food and 0.84 kilograms of oxygen each day. Even the International Space Station, which has reached 98 percent water recovery, relies on deliveries. It costs about $3 billion a year to run.

The fourth set of bumps concerns people. A resident needing a surgeon faces a trip of days to reach Earth. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, requires members to help spacecraft crews who land in distress and return them to the launching authority, which means a country or a qualifying international organization. A self-declared state appears to have no standing under it. Crime would fall under the law of the registering country, and US citizens would still owe US tax returns. A child born aboard would take nationality from whatever the parents' countries provide, because the Outer Space Treaty does not mention birth. One operator's debris endangers everyone nearby, and no one can fence off the surroundings.

A common misunderstanding is that a point with no ground and no neighbours must be free of law. In fact the law travels with the craft through its register. Another is that being first at a Lagrange point gives a right to stay there alone. Article I keeps it open to others, and a safety zone under the Accords lasts only as long as the work and binds only those who signed. A third is that declaring a nation at L5 could meet the usual test of statehood, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, which asks for a defined territory. A position in empty space that no one may claim does not provide one.

The most workable version is a licensed, registered station at or near one of these points, operated by a company under the supervision of a cooperating country. Residents could agree among themselves by contract how daily life is run, within that country's law. No published plan for a private settlement here is known. The chance of building one is estimated at about 3 percent, and the chance of holding on against outside control at about 20 percent, because supply lines to Earth and the registering country's authority stay in place the whole time.

orbital-megastructures.essay:
A megastructure, in this context, means a human-made object in space far larger than any spacecraft flown so far. Two kinds have been proposed as places to live or work. The first is the giant space habitat, a spinning wheel or cylinder in which the spin presses people against the inner wall and imitates gravity. The second is the space elevator, a cable running from the ground up into orbit, with climbing machines carrying people and cargo along it. None has been built. They raise the same legal question as any spacecraft, and the elevator raises an extra one because it touches Earth.

The Stanford torus came from a NASA summer study at Stanford University in 1975. It is a ring 1.8 kilometres across, turning once a minute, for 10,000 residents, with a total mass of about 10 million metric tons. About 95 percent of that would be a radiation shield of raw soil from the Moon, and the site would be the Earth-Moon L5 point, a stable spot in the Moon's orbit. Kalpana One, a design revised by Al Globus in 2007, is a cylinder with a 250-metre radius and a length of 325 metres for 3,000 people. The McKendree cylinder of 1995 has a 460-kilometre radius and a length of 4,600 kilometres. The Bishop Ring of 1997 has a 1,000-kilometre radius and about 3 million square kilometres of land, close to the size of India, held in by walls about 200 kilometres high and needing carbon nanotubes, a very strong material made of carbon atoms. All remain on paper.

The cost problem is simplest to see through mass. At the Falcon 9 rocket's price of about $3,246 per kilogram to low orbit, lifting the 10 million tons of a Stanford torus from Earth would cost about $32 trillion, by simple arithmetic, before any construction. That is why the design relies on Moon soil, and using it would require an industry on the Moon that does not exist. Even the 5 percent not made of soil would come to about $1.6 trillion at that rate. For comparison, the International Space Station costs about $3 billion a year to run. Large colonies have been designed since 1975 and have never been funded, so the chance of building one is estimated at about 2 percent.

The law for the habitat is short, and it does not change with size. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is the main treaty on what countries may do in space. Article VI says private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a treaty member. Article VIII says the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space. Article VII makes countries liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage caused by their space objects. Under the Liability Convention, a later treaty on that subject, a launching country pays without any need to prove fault for damage on Earth or to aircraft, and pays for damage in space if it was at fault. A launching country includes one that launches, pays for the launch, or whose territory is used. A ring with 10,000 residents would legally be the same as a small satellite with a very large crew, under one country's register. Nothing in the treaty turns an object into territory because people live on it.

A habitat built in parts by different countries could follow the International Space Station. A 1998 treaty among its partners leaves each with legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board, and no single legal authority covers the whole station.

The elevator adds a physical link to Earth. The cable is held taut by a counterweight far out in space. The stated technical obstacle is the cable material. Google X, Google's research lab, froze its project in 2014 after finding that no one had made a flawless carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre. A 2016 study by Feng Ding's team suggested small flaws could sharply cut the strength of nanotubes. Obayashi, a Japanese builder, announced in 2012 that it could build one by 2050 with an 8-day climber trip to geosynchronous orbit, where a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation. Nothing has been built.

Bradley Edwards worked from 2000 on a version with a thin ribbon, supported by NASA's advanced concepts institute. Construction would begin with a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, and 207 climbers would add material until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber. He proposed anchoring it on a movable sea platform in the western equatorial Pacific, to avoid lightning and hurricanes and to shift the ribbon out of the way of space debris large enough to track.

The sea anchor brings in ocean law. Ocean sites are usually in international waters, which could make talks over territory simpler. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, lists building artificial islands among the freedoms of the high seas, says no country may claim any part of the high seas, and says artificial islands get no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has. So an anchor at sea creates no territory. A floating platform registered as a ship flies one country's flag, and a warship may board a ship with no nationality. A land anchor would sit under the law of the country that hosts it. Above the anchor, the cable passes through the air, then space. Over a country, the air belongs to that country under the Chicago Convention, with no stated height limit, and the boundary between air and space has never been agreed. The treaties do not mention elevators at all. Whether a cable fixed to Earth counts as a "space object" is therefore uncertain, and that affects who pays if it falls. Sunao Kai of Nihon University argued in a 2012 conference paper that because an elevator runs from Earth into space, it cannot be analysed under space law alone and has to be read together with the law of the sea and the law of the air. No court or treaty body has ruled on the point. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could control most space activities.

Fundraising has been its own hazard. LiftPort Group, founded in Washington state in 2003, announced a nanotube plant in New Jersey and a goal of launching an elevator in 2010. The plant was never built, though the company did test a 1,000-foot ribbon held up by a balloon. It faced a state penalty over an alleged illegal share offering and settled without a fine in February 2010. A 2012 Kickstarter campaign raised $110,353 from 3,468 backers, and many have reportedly asked what happened and received no reply. In April 2019 its founder admitted little progress despite more than $200,000 in seed funding.

The common misunderstanding is that size eventually creates a country. A habitat with thousands of residents could meet the population test of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist of statehood, yet it would still have no land the law allows anyone to hold, and it would still be on a government's register. Another misunderstanding is that an elevator in international waters escapes all states. Its platform would need a flag, and launching countries would answer for damage. Everyone aboard either structure stays within reach of the registering country and their home country, and one operator's debris endangers all the others.

The most workable version is modest, a small licensed station registered by a cooperating country, growing in stages. Voyager Station, a proposed wheel-shaped hotel in orbit covered in its own entry, shows how far such plans have got, with no funding announced as of 2024 and no construction begun. The chance of holding out against outside control is estimated at about 12 percent, because launch licensing, liability rules and, for an elevator, the anchor all stay within a state's reach.

stratosphere-near-space.essay:
Above the heights where airliners fly and below the heights where satellites can stay in orbit lies a band of thin air that has no agreed legal name. People call parts of it the stratosphere, a layer of the atmosphere, and "near space", the band above normal aircraft and below orbit. It attracts people because it seems to sit between two legal systems. No treaty sets special rules for it, and that gap is the place to begin.

Two treaties meet here without touching. The Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, says in Article 1 that countries hold full authority over the air above their territory, and it states no height limit. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article II that no country can take over outer space, but it does not say where outer space begins. The situation resembles two neighbouring properties with no survey of the boundary between them. Over a country, this height is treated in practice as that country's airspace. Over the high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, the same freedom to fly applies as at lower heights.

People have tried to draw the boundary. The UN's space committee, COPUOS, has considered where to draw the line between air and space since 1967 without agreeing, and some countries oppose defining a line at all. Legal writers describe two camps. The spatial camp wants a fixed height, and the functional camp would classify an object by what it does. The figure most often used is the Kármán line at 100 km, named after the engineer Theodore von Kármán. It is a reference point that has not been agreed in law, according to the Library of Congress. FAI, the body that keeps air-sport records, uses it to separate aeronautics from astronautics. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in their space laws, and the US has endorsed 100 km as the point where its Air Force's and Space Force's areas of responsibility divide, according to a 2025 UN submission. The US armed forces also call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 km, an astronaut, and the astronomer Jonathan McDowell argued in 2018 for 80 km as better suited to the physics. Other proposals include 110 km (UN paper A/AC.105/L.168), and 120 km and 160 km for the top of near space. Another, put forward by Greece in its reply to the UN committee, would set the legal regime by the lowest point a satellite can reach in orbit. A UN submission states that national airspace has functionally not been legislated beyond 400,000 feet, about 122 km. That language comes from a draft treaty by the International Association for the Advancement of Space Safety, and it is not law.

The lower edge is also blurred. New Zealand defines high altitude as starting from flight level 600, an aviation measure of about 60,000 feet. Most aircraft fly below it, according to the Jakarta Post, citing the International Civil Aviation Organization. A UN submission puts flight level 600 at approximately 18 km, while the Jakarta Post says 20 km. The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for radio coordination, treats stations at 20 to 50 km as high-altitude platforms, but that definition concerns radio only.

A founder might think of this band as unclaimed. Events in 2023 show that governments do not treat it that way at the heights a balloon can reach. On 4 February 2023, American F-22 fighters shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon off South Carolina. US officials said it was between 60,000 and 65,000 feet, about 20 km up, above US territorial waters. China called this unlawful force against a civil aircraft, and the United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. An analysis from Leiden Law School reasoned that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the Chicago Convention, and that at 20 km it was in airspace and not in outer space. If it was a civil aircraft, Article 3 bis of the treaty and customary law limit the use of weapons against it. If it was a state aircraft, the treaty does not apply and the general law on steps taken in response to another state's breach does. Kuan-Wei Chen of McGill University's Institute of Air and Space Law agreed that the object was an aircraft and that at about 18 km it was clearly in the airspace of the country below. He argued differently on weapons, saying Article 3 bis was adopted after the downing of Korean Air Lines Flight 007 and is arguably limited to passenger airliners, so it may not cover an empty balloon. Satellites are treated differently. They pass over countries without permission because they have freedom of overflight, while balloons and aircraft come under aviation law and need permission to enter. These events show Article 1 being applied at about 20 km. They do not show how far up it runs.

Loon shows the peaceful route. It carried mobile network equipment about 20 km up on balloons, steered by choosing among the high-altitude winds. It started in 2011 at Google's experimental lab. It signed with Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's approval. Because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with Uganda. No country had to challenge it, because it asked first. Alphabet closed it in 2021 for lack of a viable business.

Suppose someone wanted to station a crewed platform at 30 km and declare independence. Launches and balloon flights begin on a country's soil, so the first letter would come from a national aviation authority, and a launch licence may also be needed where a rocket is involved. Balloons and high-altitude platforms need a launch site, an entry on a register and radio frequencies from a country. Under the treaty the craft takes the nationality of its register. Frequencies are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, so that member's regulator is in charge. Above the band where normal aircraft fly, a person cannot breathe the outside air, so the platform needs a sealed cabin and must carry its air, water and food, which are brought up from a country below. Sickness or a leak means coming down, in whichever country lies below or across the winds.

The hardware is far from this stage. JP Aerospace, a volunteer American group founded by John Powell, wants an inhabited floating base called a Dark Sky Station as a step towards orbit. The Register described mile-wide platforms at 140,000 feet, about 43 km, and Powell described a full-size station two miles across in 2004. So far it has built a 175-foot airship called Ascender for about $500,000 and flown an uncrewed craft called Tandem at 95,085 feet on 22 October 2011. Nobody has lived on any of it, and the group makes no claim to sovereignty. A station at that height would still sit below both the 80 km and 100 km lines. Cloud Nine, the mile-wide floating spheres drawn by Buckminster Fuller and Shoji Sadao around 1960, remained a photocollage.

Three misunderstandings recur. The first is that the lack of a treaty height leaves an empty gap, when it actually leaves each country free to say the air is its own and to act where it can. The second is that the Kármán line is law. Some bodies and some national laws use it, and no treaty does. The third is that a position over the open ocean escapes all this. The freedom to fly there belongs to countries, and the craft still needs a register, as any aircraft does, and a place to start and finish its flight.

The workable version is an uncrewed balloon or platform flown under a national licence with the consent of the countries below. No self-governing station is known at this height, and no platform here carries people for long stays. A crewed version would have the legal status of a registered aircraft. Estimates are low on building and on holding such a place, and recognition is estimated at close to nothing.

airborne-habitats.essay:
The idea of living permanently in the air appears in films and in architects' drawings, and it has never been done. Nobody lives on a flying platform today. To understand why, it helps to look at the machines that come closest and at the rules they already answer to.

The closest machines are called high-altitude platforms. These are uncrewed aircraft or airships meant to stay very high up for weeks or years, usually to carry radio equipment, so that they work a little like a very low satellite. The International Telecommunication Union, or ITU, is the UN agency that coordinates radio use, and its definition is the nearest thing to a legal description of these craft. Paragraph 1.66A of its Radio Regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a radio station on an object at 20 to 50 kilometres up, at a specified nominal fixed point relative to the Earth. That wording covers radio use only. It says nothing about who owns the air at that height, and it treats the platform as a piece of radio equipment.

Those heights lie above normal traffic. In the United States, Class A airspace, the controlled airspace used by airliners, ends at 60,000 feet, about 18 kilometres, and these platforms fly above it. The air above 60,000 feet is itself classed as Class E airspace in the United States, so it remains inside the American classification system. Above Class A there is no special legal zone. Air over a country falls under that country's rules, and no treaty sets the height where this ends. No case of anyone claiming a flying nation appears in the published descriptions of these programs.

The history of the hardware explains the physical side. Helios, a NASA solar aircraft, reached 96,863 feet on 13 August 2001 and broke up in flight in 2003. The Airbus Zephyr, a solar drone, can fly for 64 days. Facebook's Aquila drone was halted in 2018, Google's Loon balloons ended in 2021, and Titan Aerospace's Solara was shut down by 2017. Other craft named in this height band include the BAE PHASA-35 and the Kea Atmos Mk1. All of these carry equipment. None carries a person to live on.

Stratobus is the project most like a long-stay habitat, and it shows how slowly such a thing moves. It is a robotic airship designed by the French company Thales Alenia Space to hover about 20 kilometres up. In 2015 the design was 100 metres long, weighed about 5 tons and could carry 250 kilograms of equipment for five years. The company expected a couple of days on the ground each year for maintenance. It planned a prototype in 2018 or 2019 and commercial sale around 2020, and neither date was met. By 2025 it was described as 142 metres long, the company had started building two reduced-scale test models, and the aim was to be ready for use by 2031. The carrying limit matters here. A payload of 250 kilograms on a craft that large is less than the weight of three or four adults, before counting food, water, air supply or walls. No plans for people aboard have been reported.

Sky Cruise is the famous picture of the opposite end. It is an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022, based on a design by art director Tony Holmsten drawn more than a decade earlier. It shows a nuclear-powered flying hotel carrying up to 5,000 people and staying in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving on jets that land on it. Al-Ghaili suggested that small reactors expected in the 2030s might power it. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and he himself stressed that it is only a concept. No such aircraft has been built.

Suppose someone did build a crewed platform and wanted to run it as an independent place. The bumps would come in this order. Before takeoff, the craft needs safety certification and flight permission. Stratobus's makers said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, and that was for a craft with nobody aboard. Certificates come from a country, and that country's aviation authority answers for the craft. In practice, a platform answers to the aviation and radio authorities that certify it. An aircraft must be registered with a country to have legal standing under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on international civil flying, and the registering country's rules follow it.

Next come radio frequencies. A platform needs them to talk to the ground and to run any business, and frequency assignments reach the ITU through a member country, which puts that member's regulator in charge. A group with no member country behind it would have no one to file for it. Then comes the question of where the craft is. Over a country, it is in that country's air and subject to its orders. Over open ocean, no one owns the air, but the craft still carries its register's law.

After that come the physical limits. Even a platform designed for years in the air has to come down somewhere for maintenance, as Stratobus does for a couple of days a year. A place with people on it would have far greater needs, including food, water, medicine and a way to bring a sick person down. Each of those runs through an airfield in some country. Whoever controls that airfield controls the supply, which is the same weakness seen in Camp Barneo, the Arctic tourist camp that depended on Norwegian flights. Insurance, money and banking would then present the same problems as any other place outside a recognized state. A flying place with no recognized government could not license a bank, and its residents would remain citizens of their home countries, subject to their tax laws.

The business side has its own record. Several programs ended with large companies behind them, including Loon, which Alphabet closed in 2021 because it lacked a viable business. Those programs carried only equipment, with no food, water, air or medical care to pay for.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that a height above airliner traffic is a height above the law. Class A ending at 60,000 feet only marks where one airspace class stops and another, Class E, begins. In February 2023 American fighters shot down a Chinese balloon at about that height. The other is that a video of a flying city means someone is building one. Sky Cruise is an animation, and the design for it has not moved past that.

The workable version today is an uncrewed platform flown with a government's permission, carrying radio or observation equipment, on a register, using licensed frequencies. No crewed flight has been reported for these programs. A permanent home in the air remains unbuilt, and estimates for it are low on building, on law and on holding the position, because the craft would need a state's registration and somewhere to land or receive supplies.

airspace-over-high-seas.essay:
People often say that the country below owns the air. That statement is true over land and coastal waters, and it leaves out four things. No country holds authority over the air above the high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, which is about 58.6% of the sea surface. The air over Antarctica has no settled authority. No treaty sets the upper limit of airspace. An exclusive economic zone gives no airspace rights either. That zone, usually called the EEZ, is the belt up to 200 nautical miles from a coast where the coastal country controls resources. Only the territorial sea, up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, carries the air above it into the country's territory.

The rule comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Article 87(1)(b) says every country is free to fly over the high seas, and Article 58(1) applies the same freedom over the EEZ. Article 135 adds that the rules for the deep seabed, which the treaty calls the Area, do not change the legal status of the air above it. A country that controls the fish or the oil below therefore gains no right to shut the sky above them.

Antarctica works differently. The Antarctic Treaty governs the continent south of 60 degrees South, and its Article IV freezes the claims that seven countries have made to slices of the continent. Countries that do not recognize a claim therefore appear able to dispute whether the air above a claimed sector counts as the claimant's airspace. This is an interpretation, because the treaty does not address authority over airspace.

Freedom to fly here is a freedom held by countries, so it reaches a person through an aircraft that belongs to a country. Everything else follows from that. The Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, says in Articles 17 to 20 that an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it, may be on one register only, and must display that country's marks. Article 12 says each country must make sure that aircraft carrying its marks follow the rules wherever they are, and it adds that "over the high seas, the rules in force shall be those established under this Convention." The sky over the open ocean therefore has flight rules even though no country owns it. Those rules are the standards of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying.

Criminal law is handled by a second treaty. The Tokyo Convention, signed on 14 September 1963, applies to offences committed on board an aircraft in flight, including over the high seas or any other area outside every country's territory. It leaves out state aircraft used for military, customs or police work. It gives power over those offences to the state of registration, meaning the country where the aircraft is listed, and each party must make sure its law provides for this. A commander, the crew and in some cases passengers may act to prevent offences, and the commander may put an offender off the aircraft or hand them to the authorities on landing. Other countries generally may not interfere with an aircraft in flight to enforce their criminal law, with some exceptions. The arrangement resembles the rule for ships, which fall under the law of the country whose flag they fly. An aircraft flying over water no state owns therefore carries one country's legal system with it, and a registered flying platform would too.

Suppose a group builds a large long-range aircraft, stays over the middle of the Pacific, and declares that no country's law applies on board. The first problem comes before takeoff. The aircraft has to leave from an airport in some country, which will ask for its registration and its safety papers. If the group registers it, the registering country's law applies inside it, and a fight or a theft on board goes to that country's courts. If the group does not register it, it has no right to enter any country's airspace. Article 5 of the Chicago Convention gives its flight rights only to aircraft of countries that have joined, so an aircraft with no country has none of them.

That leads to the second problem, which is physical. Every aircraft has to take off and land somewhere. Fuel and maintenance force landings in a country, and on landing the crew and the craft are under that country's law. Residents of such a place would meet the same difficulties as anyone else who lands, including passports with no country code on the lists that border systems use. Food, spare parts and medical care all come through an airport in some country, under its rules on who may enter.

The third problem is that some countries reach out past their own airspace. An air defense identification zone is a stretch of sky beyond a country's airspace in which that country, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report. The United States created the first on 27 December 1950, during the Korean War, because it wanted early warning of a Soviet air attack. About 20 countries and regions now have such zones, including Canada, India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom. American policy applies its zone only to commercial aircraft intending to enter American airspace. On 23 November 2013 China declared a zone over the East China Sea, with reporting duties as far as 300 miles from its territorial waters and over islands Japan controls. Japan warned of unpredictable events, the United States objected, and South Korea expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. Legal writers disagree about these zones. One view holds that declaring one breaks no law, and another says they conflict with freedom of navigation in international airspace. No treaty authorises them, and Robert Beckman of the National University of Singapore noted in 2014 that global conventions do not expressly forbid them either. A long-staying craft near one of these coasts should expect to be asked to identify itself.

The law of the sea treaty extends its piracy rules to aircraft, so under Articles 101 and 105 a private aircraft may be seized for piracy. Under Article 110(4), military aircraft may stop and inspect a suspect ship, which is called the right of visit. Taxes on an American citizen continue under Cook v. Tait, the 1924 Supreme Court case on worldwide income. Reasoning from the same rules, an unrecognized place could sign documents, but other countries would have no duty to treat them as treaties and would be likely to see them as private papers.

Two misunderstandings are common here. One is that a place no country owns is a place no country's law reaches. The law arrives on board with the registration and travels with the passengers. The other is that the freedom to fly over the sea is a personal right. Article 87 gives it to countries, and an individual uses it through a country's register.

The workable version is an ordinary registered aircraft flying over open water, with residents following private agreements under the law of the registering country. A permanently airborne self-governing craft has not been built and would still need to be on a register. This zone gets a higher legal estimate than the air over land because no coastal country holds title here. The estimates for holding on stay low because of the landings, the registration and the identification zones, and the chance of recognition by other countries is estimated at close to nothing.

airspace-over-states.essay:
The air over a country counts as part of that country in much the same way its land does. A government decides who may fly through it, on what terms, and when they must come down. The idea of founding a separate place in the sky over someone else's land therefore starts in a difficult position, and it helps to see how this rule came about.

An old common-law saying, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, held that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. Aircraft made that saying impractical for private owners. In United States v. Causby, a 1946 decision of the American Supreme Court, a family with 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, complained about military planes passing low over their chicken farm. The end of the runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. The Court wrote that the old doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway, because otherwise every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. The family kept a narrower claim, because flights low enough to interfere with the use of the land could still count as taking their property, which requires payment. A landowner therefore cannot sell or give away the sky above a plot, because a landowner does not hold it.

Governments kept for themselves what private owners lost. The main treaty is the Chicago Convention, signed by 52 states in Chicago on 7 December 1944 and in force since 4 April 1947, the day the International Civil Aviation Organization began work. That organization is the UN agency for civil flying, and it has 193 member countries by its own count. Article 1 says every country has complete and exclusive sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the airspace above its territory. The rule continues one in the 1919 Paris Convention on air travel. Article 2 says territory means land and the coastal waters next to it. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, confirms in Article 2(2) that a coastal country's authority also covers the air above its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast.

No treaty says how high this authority goes. Later agreements have not settled it either, so balloon flights, space planes and proposals for floating cities keep raising the same question. A founder cannot rely on that gap, because governments act at heights they can reach. On 4 February 2023, American F-22 fighters shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon off South Carolina. US officials put it at 60,000 to 65,000 feet, about 20 kilometres, above US territorial waters. China called the action unlawful force against a civil aircraft, and the United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. An analysis from Leiden Law School reasoned that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the treaty, and that at 20 kilometres it was in airspace. Kuan-Wei Chen of McGill University's Institute of Air and Space Law reached the same view, saying the boundary is unsettled but a balloon at about 18 kilometres is clearly in the airspace of the country below.

The rest of the treaty shows how much a government can control. Article 6 says scheduled international flights need permission from each country flown over or landed in. Article 5 gives unscheduled flights more freedom, but only to aircraft of countries that have joined the treaty, and even then the country below may require the aircraft to land. Article 8 says pilotless aircraft need special permission. Article 9 lets a country close certain areas for military need or public safety. Article 12 says each country enforces flight rules over its territory, and also for aircraft carrying its registration marks wherever they are.

Suppose a group builds a large airship and declares it an independent nation while it floats over Kansas. The first question from any official is which country registered it. Under Articles 17 to 20, an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it, may be registered in one country only, is registered under that country's law, and must display that country's marks. The group's own register would mean nothing here, because the treaty counts only registers of member countries. If the airship stays unregistered, it appears to have no standing under the treaty at all. If the group registers it with the United States, it has accepted American rules on board. Under Articles 29 and 31, an aircraft in international flight must also carry a certificate of airworthiness, meaning an official finding that it is safe to fly, and its crew must hold licences. Those papers come from the registering country.

Moving to another country does not help, because the same problem repeats at each border. Cloud Nine, the floating spheres that the architect Buckminster Fuller and his partner Shoji Sadao drew around 1960, were meant to drift. Several thousand people would have lived inside spheres a mile wide. Nothing was built and no government was consulted, but under the Leiden reasoning a drifting city would need consent from every country below it. Loon, the internet balloon project owned by Google's parent company, shows what that means in practice. It flew about 20 kilometres up with no people aboard and a large company behind it. It signed a contract with Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's approval. Because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with neighbouring Uganda. No country had to challenge Loon, because it asked each one first.

Other problems would arrive in a rough order. A self-declared flying state could not win landing rights, since those depend on a member country standing behind the aircraft. It could rely on planes registered elsewhere, which brings that country's rules along. Radio use needs a licence. Fuel, repairs and food have to come from the ground, which means from an airport in some country, under that country's law. Passports fail as well, because the codes for issuing countries trace back to UN lists. Joining the civil aviation organization requires being a UN member or winning four-fifths of its Assembly with UN approval. Taxes follow the person. The United States taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live, as the Supreme Court held in Cook v. Tait in 1924, so an American in the air would still file a return. A person hurt or accused of a crime on board would be dealt with under the law of the registering country or the country below.

A common misunderstanding is that a government must physically reach a craft before its law applies. The treaty works the other way round. The authority exists already, and the fighter jets are only one way of enforcing it. Another is that buying land brings the sky above it. Causby shows that it brings only the protection from low flights that interfere with the land.

The workable version is an ordinary aircraft or airship, built and flown with the permission of the country below and registered under its rules. Residents could agree private rules among themselves by contract, in the way members of a club do, and that is about as far as self-rule can go. The same government that grants permission can withdraw it or order the craft down, and the arrangement lasts only while it agrees. Estimates for this zone reflect that position. Building and flying are possible, while the chance of holding any independent status over a country's own land and coastal waters is very low, because Article 1 leaves no legal room for it.
