ships-flag.essay:
People live on ships today, for years at a time, and nobody sends a warship to stop them. To see what that does and does not give a person, it helps to understand the flag.

Every ship on the high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, belongs to a country in legal terms. The flag state is the country whose flag the ship flies and whose register lists it. The system comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Nobody owns the open sea, so without some link to a country no law would reach what happens on a ship there. Under Article 90 every country, including one with no coast, may sail ships under its flag. Under Article 91 each country sets its own conditions for its flag, and there must be a "genuine link" between the country and the ship. Under Article 92(1) a ship may fly one flag only, and on the high seas only the flag state has legal power over it, except in cases set by treaty or by UNCLOS. Article 92(2) says a ship using two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having no nationality.

The register works a little like a passport for the vessel, with duties attached. Article 94 requires the flag state to keep a register and enforce rules on seaworthiness, crew and safety. Article 97 says that after a collision, only the flag state or the person's own country may bring criminal charges. Article 98 says each flag state must require captains to rescue people in danger at sea. Article 99 says any slave who reaches any ship, under any flag, is free by that fact. Open registers accept foreign-owned ships for a fee, which is why The World flies the flag of the Bahamas although it is managed from Florida. Each register sets its own limits. Liberia, for example, asks for a waiver and a willing inspection body for vessels over 20 years old.

A flag issued by a place no other country recognizes gives no protection. Article 110 lets a warship board a foreign ship if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality. The ground that matters for self-declared flags is Article 110(1)(d), having no nationality. The treaty does not mention unrecognized flags, but a court has dealt with the point. In Naim Molvan v Attorney General for Palestine, decided on 20 April 1948, the Privy Council, the British Empire's top court of appeal, considered the Asya, a ship stopped on 27 March 1946. It flew no flag, then a Turkish flag it could not show it was entitled to, then a Zionist flag. Lord Simonds wrote that freedom of the open sea is "freedom of ships which fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a State which is within the comity of nations". The Zionist flag was not the flag of any state in being, so no state could claim protection for the ship, and the court held that seizing it breached no international law. That is one British ruling from before UNCLOS. Article 110 itself speaks of boarding and checking, and how much further a warship may go against such a ship is not spelled out there. US law, for one, calls a vessel "without nationality" in several situations, including when the country named denies the registry, and applies its drug law to such vessels (46 USC 70502). Full protection from boarding by other countries applies only to warships and government ships not used for trade, under Articles 95 and 96.

Registering is the easy route. Suppose a group buys a used cruise ship and registers it. They live under that country's law on board, and it can remove them from its register. A ship can only be sovereign in the legal sense if a country stands behind it, which brings the project back to the need for recognition by other countries. The first test comes from insurers, as MS Satoshi shows. Ocean Builders bought a 1991 cruise ship in 2020 to anchor in the Gulf of Panama. Protection and indemnity insurance, the liability cover owners need against claims at sea, was not available. The company said the closest offer was a $1 million premium for $5 million of cover. It asked Panama to class the ship as non-seagoing, which would have removed about 32 of 35 treaties, and Panama refused because it had an engine and a flag. Without insurance there could be no crew, which meant losing class, the safety rating from an inspection body, and then the flag. The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020, but it was not broken up. It stayed at Panama until March 2021, when a British Virgin Islands company bought it for a cruise start-up, and Ambassador Cruise Line put it back into service in 2022 as the Ambience.

Maintenance and money come next. Villa Vie Odyssey was a 30-year-old ship sold as a home, with cabins from $99,999 plus monthly fees. It sat for months in a Belfast yard before sailing on 30 September 2024. On 26 October 2026 at Sihanoukville in Cambodia, the chief executive told residents to leave because the company could not secure fuel, and more than 200 went ashore. He said the company would file for Chapter 11, the US bankruptcy process. Residents held a contract with a company, so their home depended on that company's money. Life at Sea Cruises sold a three-year voyage with no ship and cancelled in November 2023. By January 2024 only four passengers had refunds, and 78 customers asked US prosecutors to investigate about $16 million in deposits. How that ended is not known. Blueseed, a startup ship planned off California to avoid work visas, never raised the $18 million it needed. Freedom Ship, a plan for 80,000 people, has seen its estimate rise from $6 billion to as much as $20 billion, and Pangeos, at $8 billion, remains a design. MS The World is the working model. It was completed in 2002 and has 165 residences owned by residents, who elect an advisory board.

Women on Waves, a Dutch group, takes women to international waters to give abortion pills under the law of its Dutch flag and a Dutch permit. Portuguese warships blocked it in 2004, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in February 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression. Guatemala's army blocked the pier within 24 hours of docking. A flag gives no right to enter a port.

Coastal states have also learned to reach ships through the shore. Radio Mercur broadcast to Denmark until a 1962 law banned supporting it. Radio Nord flew Nicaragua's flag until Sweden pressed Nicaragua, and moved to Panama, and then Sweden banned selling its advertising. It closed in 1962. Radio Veronica and Radio North Sea International, whose ship Mebo II was firebombed in 1971, closed under a Dutch law of 1974. Radio Caroline kept going from international waters after Britain's 1967 Act made it illegal for British subjects to supply or advertise on it, until fuel and supplies ran out in 1990. The gambling ship SS Rex, off Santa Monica, won an appeal over how to measure a bay, and in 1939 California's Attorney General, Earl Warren, raided it as a public nuisance. On 20 November 1939, in People v. Stralla, the California Supreme Court held that Santa Monica Bay is a bay inside the state's boundary, measured from a line between Point Vicente and Point Dume, so the Rex had been anchored within state jurisdiction. It upheld the conviction of Harold Adams on that ground. The broadcasting laws left the ships alone and went after the people on land who supplied them and sold their advertising. Sea Shepherd adds another warning. In 2013 a US appeals court called its attacks on whalers piracy, holding that "private ends" means more than money, and piracy opens a ship to any warship regardless of flag. The court later held the group in contempt, it agreed in 2015 to pay $2.55 million, and a settlement announced on 23 August 2016 permanently barred it and its founder Paul Watson from attacking the whalers or coming within 500 yards of their ships on the open sea.

The United States still taxes its citizens wherever they live under Cook v. Tait, and banks report accounts. A resident arriving in port falls under that port's law, and specialist medical care means going ashore. A child born at sea normally takes nationality from the parents. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which 82 countries had joined as of January 2025, treats the birth as happening in the flag country only if the child would otherwise be stateless.

A common misunderstanding is that a flag creates a country. A flag gives a ship a nationality, and a government can withdraw it, which is why Swedish pressure on Nicaragua pushed Radio Nord's owners to Panama. Another is that a registered ship is lawless at sea, when the flag state's law applies. The workable version is an ordinary registered ship run by a solid company, with a private ownership agreement, as The World has. Living there is estimated as very achievable, while recognition as a state is estimated at close to nothing, because residents trade independence for stability.

central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard.essay:
The Arctic has two very different places that a founder might think about, and it helps to keep them apart. One is the central Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, which is open sea covered by moving ice. The other is Svalbard, a group of real islands about twice the size of Belgium, where people from many countries can live without a visa. Neither place offers independence.

Begin with the ocean. It is high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, surrounded by the coastal resource zones of five countries, Canada, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Russia and the United States. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, applies there, and the same limits apply as on any high seas. No one may claim the water, and a vessel needs a flag or it can be boarded. There is also a treaty on fishing. The Agreement to Prevent Unregulated High Seas Fisheries in the Central Arctic Ocean was concluded at Ilulissat, Greenland, on 3 October 2018 and took effect for Canada on 25 June 2021. Under Articles 1 and 13 it covers the single area of high seas surrounded by those five countries and runs for 16 years, with five-year renewals. Its opening text says ice has generally covered this water all year, though the ice is shrinking.

The seabed below may not be free at all. Under Article 76 of UNCLOS, a coastal country's continental shelf, the seabed it controls for resources, can reach past 200 nautical miles within set limits. The seabed under the central Arctic can therefore belong to a coastal country and fall outside the international deep seabed. Russia's 2007 expedition shows how this works and how it does not. Two small Mir submarines planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the Pole, at 4,261 metres, under the expedition leader Artur Chilingarov. Canada's foreign minister Peter MacKay answered that this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory, and a US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-nautical-mile zones of the five coastal countries leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question, which is an unofficial figure. He said any country wanting that seabed has to build a scientific case under the treaty, and he called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim. A private flag would have no more effect. Greenpeace lowered its own flag to the same seabed in April 2013, with a capsule holding nearly three million signatures asking for a global sanctuary. The European Parliament has called for a sanctuary too, and none has been created.

The scientific process has moved on since the 2007 dive. The Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf is the UN expert body that reviews these cases. On 6 February 2023 it issued recommendations on Russia's Arctic submission, agreeing that the Lomonosov Ridge, the Mendeleev-Alpha Rise and the Podvodnikov Basin are natural extensions of Russia's shelf and finding its evidence on the Gakkel Ridge insufficient. Russia filed a revised submission on 14 February 2023. Denmark for Greenland and Canada filed their own Arctic submissions in 2013 to 2014 and in 2019, which the commission had not yet considered as of March 2023, and they run towards the same area near the North Pole. The commission does not settle overlaps, so the countries have to negotiate them, and the coastal country sets its own final limits. Any seabed left beyond the final boundaries would be the international deep seabed, run by the International Seabed Authority.

Physically, the ocean is very hard to live on. It offers moving ice and no local supplies. The one legal test comes from a research camp. T-3, a drifting iceberg about 11 by 5 kilometres, was a staffed American station from 1952 to 1978. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey, during a dispute over raisin wine. The island lay within the sector Canada claimed, and Canada took no action. American officials flew him to Virginia and tried him under the special American law for crimes at sea. A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law applied there, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place, and it overturned the conviction for other trial errors. He was acquitted at a new trial. Congress settled the question of legal authority over such a place in 1984. Living on the ice therefore did not put anyone beyond a court.

Now turn to Svalbard. Until the 20th century it was terra nullius, land belonging to no state. Whalers and then miners from many countries worked there with almost no law, and disputes between miners and owners created demand for a government. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty was the answer, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925. It began with 14 parties and has 49 members as of 2026, according to Wikipedia. Article 1 recognizes Norway's "full and absolute sovereignty". Articles 2 and 3 give nationals of member countries equal rights to fishing, hunting, access, trade and mining, subject to local law. Article 8 says taxes must be spent on Svalbard itself, and mining rules cannot favor anyone. Article 9 says no naval base or fortification may be built. Russia uses its rights through its settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden, and about 2,500 people live on the islands.

Many people hear "no visa" and assume Svalbard is a kind of free zone. The Governor of Svalbard, Norway's local official, explains otherwise. Norway's Immigration Act does not apply there, so a foreigner needs no Norwegian visa or residence permit, though someone needing a Schengen visa must have one to travel through mainland Norway, and a double-entry visa to come back. Everyone must carry a valid travel document. Under Norway's rejection and expulsion regulations for Svalbard, people must have the means to live there, and the Governor may reject those who do not. This applies to Norwegians and foreigners alike. Those planning to come are advised to obtain work and housing first. Most housing belongs to employers, so it is hard to get housing without a job. The Norwegian state owns practically all land, and in practice it is not possible to buy a plot to build a home. Private boats and planes must send advance notice of passengers and crew. Living there gives no rights to govern. Norwegian law and the Governor apply. Under rules announced in 2022, non-Norwegians must have lived three years in a Norwegian municipality to vote or stand in Longyearbyen's local elections, and time on Svalbard does not count, which could affect over 700 of the 2,500 people there.

Suppose a group of friends moved to Longyearbyen, the main town, and announced a self-governing community. They would need jobs and homes from existing employers, and they could rent and trade like anyone else. Their declaration would have no effect, because 49 countries have recognized Norway's sovereignty in the treaty. If they could not support themselves, the Governor could send them away.

Older Arctic cases show what happens to those who try to take land. Norway itself tried in 1931 to occupy part of eastern Greenland, calling it Erik the Red's Land and arguing it belonged to no state. On 5 April 1933 the Permanent Court of International Justice ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. In 1921 Vilhjalmur Stefansson sent five settlers to Wrangel Island, north of Siberia, to claim it for Canada. A relief ship failed in 1922, three set out for Siberia and vanished, one died of scurvy, and Ada Blackjack survived alone until rescue in August 1923. A new party of 13 was removed by a Soviet ship in 1924, and its leader, Charles Wells, and two children died. Hans Island, a bare rock of 1.3 square kilometres, was divided peacefully by Canada, Denmark and Greenland on 14 June 2022 after decades in which each side raised flags and left gifts.

The workable version is simple and limited. An ordinary person from a member country can move to Svalbard, if they can support themselves, and live and do business under Norwegian law. In the central ocean, a registered ship or a government-backed camp is possible for short periods. The legal estimate for this zone is moderate because of those open rights, and the holding estimate is low because no one can govern there.

floating-ice.essay:
Ice that floats in the sea is hard for the law to classify. A person can walk on it and build a hut, as on land, and it also moves with the currents and melts. Who owns a floating iceberg has no settled answer.

It helps to separate three kinds of floating ice. Sea ice forms when the ocean surface freezes. An ice shelf is a thick sheet of floating ice still attached to land, like those around Antarctica. An iceberg or ice island is a large piece that has broken off a glacier or shelf and drifts free.

Legal writers take three views of an iceberg floating free. The first says it belongs to no one, which lawyers call res nullius, so the first to take it may keep it, much as a fisherman keeps a fish. The second says it can be held under a claim by a country. The third says it is shared by all, which is called res communis, in the way the open sea is shared. In a 2022 article in the law journal Ius Novum, Mateusz Osiecki argues that an iceberg floating free in Antarctic waters is no country's property and sits on the high seas, so taking and towing it would probably not breach any country's territorial rights. That is one writer's reasoning, and no court has ruled on it. C. Wood-Donnelly, writing in Marine Policy in 2022, describes iceberg harvesting as unregulated and its legal status in international law as limited to the "rule of capture", which is close to the first view.

Nearer the coast the answer is firmer. Matthew Paterson, writing in 2019, says icebergs in a territorial sea fall under the coastal country's laws, and he suggests that in the wider resource zone they may count as natural resources under its sovereign rights. Canada is the one state he found regulating them. In Newfoundland and Labrador, six companies were reported to hold licences, paying the province a fee based on volume after locals objected to a flat $5,000 charge. Paterson also argues that Article 7 of the 1991 Environmental Protocol, which bars mineral resource activities in Antarctica other than scientific research, could stop commercial harvesting there if "mineral" is read in its scientific sense, and he notes that the dictionary sense makes this debatable.

Location adds another layer. The Antarctic Treaty, under its Article VI, covers everything south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, without taking away rights any country has on the high seas in that area. An ice shelf is therefore treated like part of Antarctica, with its frozen claims and its rules. Paterson, citing the writer Joyner, suggests that a shelf frozen to the seabed should be treated as land and otherwise as part of the sea. A berg that has drifted north of that line is simply floating in the ocean. A towing ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. Osiecki notes that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has joined neither the Antarctic Treaty System nor the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, which leaves open how far those rules bind a UAE-flagged tow. He also sets out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty.

The one court that has come near this question did so after a killing. T-3, also called Fletcher's Ice Island, was a drifting iceberg in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as a staffed American research station from 1952 to 1978, with huts, a power plant and an airstrip. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla, armed with a borrowed rifle during a dispute over raisin wine, shot and killed the station manager, Bennie Lightsey. The island then lay in the Arctic sector Canada claimed, but Canada chose not to act and said this did not affect its claims. American officials flew Escamilla to Virginia and charged him, arguing that the ice was on the high seas and so within the special American law for crimes at sea. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, split evenly on whether American law covered an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place. The conviction was overturned for other errors, and he was acquitted at a new trial. Congress did not settle the question until a change to federal law in 1984. The shooting on unclaimed ice did not fall outside all law. A national government took the suspect home, and the argument was about which statute applied.

Physically, the record shows that people can live on ice for weeks or years with heavy support, and never permanently. On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on a floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole. Four men lived there for nine months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, until icebreakers took them off in February 1938. From 1954, one to three stations ran each year. A typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years, until its floe reached the Greenland Sea, and North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. Some 800 people have drifted on these stations since 1937, with crews replaced each year. All were run by one government body, the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice thawed too fast. Russia therefore ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform in 2017, completed in August 2022, which ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024 and started NP-42 in 2024.

Antarctic ice has given its own warning. The iceberg A23a broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986 and carried off part of the Soviet base Druzhnaya I, which stood on that part of the shelf. Rusted debris from the base could still be seen in the ice in January 2025. A23a measured about 3,500 square kilometres in January 2025, when it was the largest iceberg in the world. By March 2026 it was down to 180 square kilometres, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so.

Suppose a private group sets up on a floe and declares it a country. The first thing it needs is an aircraft or ship, and the base for that is in some country. Camp Barneo shows what follows. It was a private tourist camp near the North Pole, founded in 2002 by the Russian Alexander Orlov, with visits from about $20,000. Because the ice keeps moving, it had to be rebuilt from nothing every April, and in 2007 winds pushed it at 0.8 kilometres an hour. Every trip from 2002 to 2017 started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, so it relied on Norway. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight ban, which it later lifted. A Russia-Ukraine dispute stopped tourist flights in 2019, COVID-19 cancelled two seasons, Russia's invasion of Ukraine ended plans for 2022, and a 2024 season was cancelled. The camp last operated in 2018. No one needs to board the ice to stop a camp, because restricting the flights is enough.

The other bumps follow from that. A camp without a government behind it has no icebreaker to rescue it when the floe cracks. Its residents remain citizens of their home countries, with the same taxes and the same criminal law. It has no fixed address for a bank, an insurer or a land title, since the ground itself drifts and may melt. The Montevideo Convention, the 1933 treaty that defines a state, asks for a defined territory, which a melting floe struggles to offer.

Building a stronger iceberg has been tried on paper. Project Habakkuk was a British wartime plan by Geoffrey Pyke for a floating airbase made of ice. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that natural icebergs have too little surface above water for an airstrip and can roll over. The idea moved on to pykrete, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp, and a ship 600 metres long. Pykrete sagged unless cooled to minus 16 degrees Celsius, the estimate rose from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and the board called the ship impractical in December 1943. The UAE Iceberg Project, announced in 2017 by Abdulla Alsheni at an estimated $100 to 150 million, aimed only to tow a berg from near Heard Island to Fujairah for water, and no tow is known to have taken place.

The workable version is a temporary camp or research station with a country or a large company behind it, supplied by air or ship, lasting a season to a few years. It gives no title and no self-rule. Estimates put the chance of building a lasting place very low, while the legal estimate is moderate only because the law is unsettled.

new-land.essay:
Now and then a volcano or an earthquake pushes new ground above the sea, or a river delta piles up a sandbar. This looks like an opening, because the ground is brand new and no one has ever lived on it. Many people assume that new land belongs to whoever gets there first. In practice the answer depends on where the ground rises and how long it lasts.

Start with the old rule on unclaimed land. For centuries a country could gain land that belonged to no one, called terra nullius, by actually occupying and governing it. In the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928, between the United States and the Netherlands, the arbitrator Max Huber held that discovery alone does not settle ownership, and that a continuous and peaceful display of state authority wins over a mere first finding. That method was one used by countries. A private person who plants a flag gets nothing from it directly, and a country must then keep governing the place.

Most new ground never reaches that question, because the sea around it is already spoken for. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, Article 2 gives a coastal country full authority over its territorial sea, the belt reaching up to 12 nautical miles from its coast, and over the seabed below. A volcano that surfaces there rises on ground that country already holds. New land is therefore almost always the property of the country whose waters it rises in. Zalzala Koh shows the simple case. It appeared off Pakistan on 24 September 2013, within hours of a 7.7-magnitude earthquake, about 2 kilometres from shore near Gwadar. It lay inside Pakistan's territorial sea, so no one else could have claimed it.

Further out the law becomes less clear. Between 12 and 200 nautical miles lies the exclusive economic zone, the belt where the coastal country controls resources, and its rights to the seabed there concern resources and do not amount to full ownership. Article 60 gives the coastal country control of artificial islands in that zone, but it does not directly address a natural island that appears. A coastal country would very likely claim such an island at once, but the treaty does not spell out the answer. Beyond national zones, Article 137 says no country may claim or take over any part of the deep seabed, and whether that reaches a natural island rising from it has not been tested. Writers set out the choices without settling them. When a new island appeared near Tonga in 2006, Duncan Hollis, writing on the law blog Opinio Juris, expected Tonga to claim it and deny that it could be land belonging to no one. If such an island lay outside a country's territory, he asked whether terra nullius should revive, with countries competing by discovery or effective occupation, or whether it should be treated as the common heritage of mankind. He wrote that attempts by private finders to found a nation rarely succeed in the modern era, though they may have a stronger claim to private property interests. Paweł Czubik, in a book chapter on islands born from the sea, calls an island in an area of limited sovereign rights the most problematic case. Land rising from a seabed no one holds has only one tested case, and the land sank before any claim succeeded.

That case is Graham Island. It rose about 30 kilometres south of Sicily in July 1831. By 17 July a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, had landed and planted an oar to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. By 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy had claimed it for Britain and named it after Sir James Graham. King Ferdinand II sent a warship and called it Ferdinandea, a French geologist named it Julia, and Spain declared an interest. At its largest it was about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high. It was loose ash, and by 17 December officials reported no trace, so that it was gone by January 1832 and the dispute lapsed unsettled. Its summit now lies about 6 metres under water, and when it stirred in 2000 and 2002, Italians placed a flag and a plaque on the bank to head off future claims.

The speed of government is the first lesson of these cases. In 1963 the eruption that made Surtsey began off the south coast of Iceland on 14 November. On 6 December three French journalists from Paris Match landed, stayed about 15 minutes and jokingly claimed it for France, and Iceland immediately said it was Icelandic. In 1965, while the eruption was still going on, Iceland declared the island a nature reserve so that scientists could watch life arrive. The eruption ended on 5 June 1967, with the highest point at 174 metres. Hard lava had capped the ash, so the island lasted. Only a few scientists may land, and no one has been able to settle there. Japan's Nishinoshima, about 940 kilometres south-southeast of Tokyo, went the same way. A fishing boat reported smoke on 30 May 1973, the Japan Coast Guard flew over that day, and the new land merged with an island Japan already held, as did more ground from 2013 onward.

The second lesson is that the ground rarely lasts. Graham Island lasted about six months and Zalzala Koh about three years, sinking 3 metres in its first month and gone by the end of 2016. Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai, in Tonga, joined in 2015, and the merged island reached 149 metres and acquired ferns and seabirds before the eruption of January 2022 destroyed most of it, leaving small remnants. Fonuafoʻou, whose name means new land, appeared on 14 October 1885, grew through several eruptions, collapsed in 1949 and is now 17 metres under water. Anything built on such ground would be lost with it.

Sandbars add a dispute of their own. South Talpatti, which India called New Moore, formed in the Bay of Bengal after the cyclone of November 1970. It never rose above 2 metres. India and Bangladesh both claimed it, because the border follows the main channel of the nearby river, and India reportedly raised its flag in 1981. It had gone by about March 2010. In the Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration, a panel of judges chosen to settle the dispute drew the sea boundary in 2014 and left the site of the vanished island on the Indian side. The dispute ran for decades between two governments, over ground that no longer existed when it ended.

Suppose a group does get to a new island first, in waters that no one has clearly claimed. It lands by boat, which comes from a port, and plants a flag. Within days a government asks what it is doing, as happened in 1831 and 1963. If it stays, it has to haul in all its water and food, since new ash holds neither. Its huts stand on loose material that waves wear down. A government can remove it, as Tonga did at Minerva, or declare a reserve, as Iceland did at Surtsey. Its home countries still tax its members and can prosecute them. No bank or insurer has a legal owner to deal with, because nobody can show title.

Three misunderstandings are common. The first is that a person can claim new land by landing on it, when that method belongs to countries. The second is that building up a reef or sandbar makes an island. Article 121(1) says an island is land that formed naturally, has water all round it and stays above water at high tide. Article 60(8) says artificial islands are not islands in law, with no territorial sea and no effect on sea boundaries. Whether a country could still hold one as territory is argued. Imogen Saunders wrote in 2021 that the question remains unanswered and that neither the doctrine of territory nor UNCLOS prevents artificial islands from being territory. That argument concerns countries and gives a private group nothing directly. The Republic of Minerva, whose backers piled sand on a South Pacific reef in 1971, was claimed and taken over by Tonga in 1972. The third is that any island brings a large sea zone with it. Under Article 121(3), rocks that cannot support people living there or an economy of their own get no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf, the seabed rights a coast normally carries.

There is no real workable version for a founder. The realistic options are visiting as a scientist or tourist, where permitted, or watching from a small plane as visitors do at Surtsey. Estimates are low for building, because new ground washes away, and low for holding it, because a government arrives quickly.

undersea-water-column.essay:
A habitat under the sea is hard to see, and some people expect it to be hard for the law to reach. In law, depth changes very little. The water and the sea floor follow the zone at the surface above them, and being underwater does not create a separate legal space.

The ocean has layers of law, under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. In the territorial sea, the belt up to 12 nautical miles from a coast, the coastal country has full authority over water and seabed, and submarines must travel on the surface and show a flag (Article 20). Further out, the seabed is usually a country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor extending from its coast. Article 77 gives that country exclusive rights to the shelf's resources, and Article 80 applies Article 60, so artificial islands, and installations with an economic purpose or that could interfere with its rights, need its permission. Further out still, the water above is high seas, the open ocean outside any country's control, while the bottom is "the Area", the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). Article 137 bars anyone from taking any part of it. Article 147 applies ISA rules to installations used for mining, so it does not appear to clearly reach a habitat with no mining.

So a person must first ask whether the habitat moves. A moving craft would likely count as a vessel. High-seas freedoms apply to the water (Articles 86 and 87), so a submerged vessel under a flag appears to be treated as a ship, although UNCLOS does not define "ship". A flag means a real country's registration, and that country's law comes aboard. Without one, the rule in Article 110 on boarding a vessel with no flag still applies to a submarine, though a warship has to find it first. Hiding is a practical advantage only, and it ends at every port call. It can also be a crime in itself. A US law, 18 USC 2285, makes it an offence, with up to 15 years in prison, to operate or embark in a submersible vessel without nationality that travels beyond a single country's territorial sea with the intent to evade detection.

A fixed habitat is the harder question. On a continental shelf it needs the coastal country's permission where Article 60 applies, and any anchor appears to give that country a physical point of contact. Research installations follow the rules of the zone where they sit, have no island status, and get safety zones of 500 metres at most (Articles 258 to 260). On the deep seabed, taking any part as your own is barred, and the ISA's rules on installations are written for mining. The treaty gives no clear answer on whether a stationary habitat tethered to the seabed counts as a ship or an installation, and the question appears open. Article 87 lists among high seas freedoms the building of artificial islands and other installations "permitted under international law", which leaves what is permitted to be worked out elsewhere. Since 17 January 2026 a further treaty applies among its members, the BBNJ Agreement on marine life outside national waters. Its Article 28 requires each member to assess the likely effects on the marine environment of planned activities under its jurisdiction or control in those areas before authorising them. Reading that text, it seems a habitat run under a member's flag or by its companies would be caught if it met the treaty's thresholds. The seafloor reaches more than 8 km deep in the Mariana Trench, according to the ISA, while the deepest habitat described below went to 610 feet off a coast.

To see why it stays shallow, it helps to understand saturation diving. Water pressure forces breathing gases into the body, and after long enough at depth the body reaches a steady state. Divers in that state can work outside for hours, and they need to decompress, returning slowly to surface pressure, only once at the end of the mission. They cannot simply swim up in an emergency. A sick person in a habitat therefore has a slow trip to any hospital.

The history starts with governments. Jacques Cousteau's Conshelf experiments put two divers, Albert Falco and Claude Wesly, on the sea floor off Marseille in 1962, with accounts differing between 10 metres for seven days and 12 metres for two weeks, and in 1963 placed six people 10 metres down in the Red Sea off Sudan for 30 days. Air, water, food and power all came from a large team on the surface. Part of the money came from French petrochemical firms, and later work showed that robots and divers from the surface could do industrial jobs more efficiently, so companies lost the reason to pay for people on the bottom. The US Navy's SEALAB I went to 192 feet off Bermuda in 1964. SEALAB II followed in 1965 off California, where Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30 days. SEALAB III went to 610 feet in February 1969, 18 months late and $3 million over budget, and the aquanaut Berry Cannon died during a repair. A Navy inquiry found his breathing equipment lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, and a 2024 study by an ocean engineer pointed to electrocution. The programme was halted.

What has lasted operates under a coastal country. Aquarius sits 62 feet down, 5.4 miles off Key Largo in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government. Built in 1986 and placed there in 1993, it was owned by the US ocean agency NOAA, and Florida International University took over operations in 2013. Jules' Undersea Lodge, a former research laboratory, is in a lagoon at Key Largo with a dock and a gift shop, and it is a building under water to which state and federal law apply. DEEP, a private UK-based company, installed its prototype Vanguard at Tennessee Reef in the same sanctuary in June 2026, designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more, and it was working toward classification by DNV, a body that certifies marine equipment. Its planned Sentinel modules would hold six people each at 200 metres for 28 days. Because they can be moved, a different country's permission would apply at each site.

The plans further out have not been built. Proteus, proposed by Fabien Cousteau for a marine park off Curaçao with government backing, was reported to need US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for three years, and in October 2024 it was still in planning. Ocean Spiral, a 2014 design by Shimizu Corporation, described 5,000 people in linked spheres at ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion, and expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay. Aquatica, proposed by Dennis Chamberland, a former NASA bioengineer, spoke of children born under water with schools and hospitals. Its first step, a four-person house called Leviathan, is not known to have been placed, and the plan named no site or legal basis. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely lie on some country's shelf.

Suppose a family wanted to live on such a habitat beyond any permit. Surface boats would have to bring food, gas and spare parts from a port, and that port's country sets the terms. Children would need birth records and schooling from somewhere. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. Crime on board would come under the law of the flag country or of the people's own countries, since US law, for one, reaches any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation for offenses by or against US nationals.

The main misunderstanding is that depth brings legal shelter. Nothing in UNCLOS gives it. A second is that living on the bottom earns a claim to it. SEALAB, Conshelf and Aquarius all kept people on the sea floor for long periods and gained no rights to the seabed. A third is that a habitat is a territory for the purposes of statehood. Research installations have no island status, and the Montevideo Convention of 1933, the usual checklist for a state, asks for a defined territory and a permanent population. Staying long term also depends on supply from the surface.

The most workable version is the one that exists, a licensed habitat for research, training or tourism in a coastal country's waters, staffed in rotation and supplied from shore. Going deeper or further out adds cost and risk and brings no new legal shelter, and the habitat's position remains that of a licensed structure under the country above it.

deep-seabed-area.essay:
Beyond the continental shelves, the seabed that extends out from each country's coast, lies the deep ocean floor. By the International Seabed Authority's own figure, this area covers about 54% of the total area of the world's oceans. In law it is called "the Area". Nobody can own it.

The reason goes back to minerals. By the 1970s companies were preparing to collect manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps of metal on the deep floor, and no treaty said who could mine there. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the 1982 treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, answered by declaring the Area and its resources the "common heritage of mankind" (Article 136), meaning they belong to humanity as a whole. A shared fund run by one body for all its members works in a similar way, since no member may take a slice for itself.

Article 137 sets out the core rule. No country may claim authority over any part of the Area, no country or person may take any part of it as their own, and no such claim or taking will be recognized. Rights in the resources belong to humanity as a whole, and minerals can be sold only under the rules of the International Seabed Authority (ISA), based in Jamaica (Article 137(2)-(3)). The ISA is the body through which member countries control activities in the Area, and all UNCLOS members belong to it (Articles 156 and 157). It was set up on 16 November 1994. It had 172 members as of 6 February 2026, made up of 171 countries plus the European Union.

Other rules fill in the picture. The status of the water and air above stays the same (Article 135), so the water remains high seas, open ocean outside any country's control. The Area is open to use for peaceful purposes only (Article 141). Archaeological and historical objects found there are to be preserved or disposed of for the benefit of humanity (Article 149). Installations used for mineral activities must be placed and removed under ISA rules, and they "do not possess the status of islands", so they cannot have a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water (Article 147(2)).

To mine, an operator needs sponsorship from a member country and an approved plan of work (Article 153). A sponsor is a country that takes responsibility for the operator. This requirement closes the obvious route for a new state, since a self-declared country cannot sponsor itself. It is not a member, so it would have to find a real one willing to answer for it, and that puts the operation under that country's supervision.

Suppose a group sent down a submersible, placed a marker on the sea floor and announced a new country on it. A submersible visit needs no ISA permission if it is only a visit, because the ISA's control concerns mineral activities. The marker gives no title. Article 137 says the claim will not be recognized, so the group would hold a piece of equipment on the sea floor with no legal right to exclude others. If the group then started collecting nodules, it would be taking something that belongs to humanity as a whole, and anyone buying the metal would be dealing outside the ISA's rules.

Deepsea Ventures tried a careful version in 1974, before the treaty existed. This American company, of Gloucester Point, Virginia, wanted the nodules in a deposit of 60,000 square kilometres in the northeastern Pacific. On 15 November its president, John Flipse, sent a notice of discovery to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, asked for diplomatic protection, and recorded a copy at a local courthouse. It claimed exclusive rights to mine and sell, and it said it was claiming no territory. It promised production within 15 years. The 1982 treaty later put the area under the authority, mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it.

Today the working system is contracts. The ISA lists 15-year exploration contracts with 22 contractors. Its text counts 19 for nodules, 7 for sulphides and 5 for crusts, 31 in all, although its sulphide sub-count adds up to 8, so the page is not fully consistent. Most are in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico. Only exploration is allowed so far. The rules for exploitation, meaning commercial mining, known as the Mining Code, were still unfinished after the July 2026 session of the ISA Council. The March 2026 Council approved no commercial mining, with benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. In July the Council asked its staff for a roadmap and a new negotiating text, and the draft decision says commercial mining should not take place without rules.

The Metals Company shows the main challenge to this system. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011, and its subsidiaries hold ISA exploration contracts, NORI sponsored by Nauru and TOML sponsored by Tonga. In June 2021 Nauru told the ISA it meant to begin mining, which started a two-year deadline to finish the rules, and the rules were not finished. The US has not joined the UNCLOS deep-sea mining system. It has a rival route, the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the US agency NOAA to speed up permits under that law, and four days later the company's American arm applied. On 9 March 2026 NOAA found the application to be in "substantial compliance", and on 19 August 2026 it published the company's consolidated application for an exploration licence and a commercial recovery permit. NOAA held a virtual public hearing on 13 October, and comments closed on 19 October with 1,663 received. Its page, last updated on 16 October 2026, listed no commercial recovery permit as issued. A separate exploration application was certified on 26 May 2026, and in August NOAA announced that it would prepare an environmental impact statement for it. The ISA's commission is investigating whether this breaches contractors' duties. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal ordered the ISA to respect fair procedure in the inquiry, without suspending it. Two days later the Council extended NORI's contract to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending. The main case is undecided. If this route succeeds, it would give mining rights under one country's law and no territory to anyone.

Ordinary diving cannot reach these depths, so every visit needs a specialised vessel and submersible, and the seafloor elsewhere reaches more than 8 km. Food, power and rescue would all come from the surface, and rescue ends in some other country's port. Nothing built here would have island status. Any investor offered shares in a seabed nation would be buying a claim that Article 137 says will not be recognized, and securities law has been used against offers of that kind on the shallower reefs.

Common misunderstandings come from the mining news. A mining contract is a licence for a set activity for a set period, and it gives no ownership of the seabed. A US permit, if issued, would not make the patch American. The ISA's installation rules do not clearly reach a habitat with no mining, and that gap gives no permission, since Article 137 still bars taking any part of the floor as one's own.

The most workable activity is to take part in the system. A company can seek a sponsoring member country and an exploration contract, or a research group can work from a flagged ship under its flag country's law. Since 17 January 2026, members of the BBNJ Agreement, a treaty on marine life outside national waters, must also assess planned activities under their jurisdiction or control in these areas before authorising them. What it gains is a contract right to explore. It gains no land, no people under its own law and no legal basis for a state.
